slides.narration: A pressure cooker whistles, a bicycle pump warms up, a refrigerator hums. Thermodynamics is the science of how energy moves between a system and its surroundings as heat and work. In this part we define temperature through thermal equilibrium, meet internal energy, state the first law, and see why a gas needs more heat to warm up at constant pressure than at constant volume.

slides.heading: Thermal equilibrium
slides.body_md: A **system** is the part of the world we study; everything else is its **surroundings**.
bullets: Two systems are in **thermal equilibrium** when, placed in contact, no net heat flows between them: their state variables stop changing.
An **adiabatic wall** blocks heat; a **diathermic wall** lets heat through.
Separated by an adiabatic wall, two systems can be at different temperatures and stay so.
Joined by a diathermic wall, they settle at a **common temperature**: that is what thermal equilibrium means.

rows: Adiabatic wall (thick foam, a vacuum flask)
Each system keeps its own temperature
Heat flows until the two reach one common temperature: thermal equilibrium

visual.alt: Table comparing adiabatic and diathermic walls and what happens to the temperatures of the systems they separate

slides.narration: A system is the part of the universe we are studying. Two systems in contact are in thermal equilibrium when no net heat flows between them any more. A thick foam wall, called adiabatic, stops heat. A thin copper sheet, called diathermic, lets heat pass until both systems settle at one common temperature.

slides.heading: The zeroth law and temperature
slides.body_md: Two blocks, A and B, are each placed against a thermometer C and give the same reading.
bullets: **Zeroth law:** if A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
**Temperature** is the property that has the same value for all systems in thermal equilibrium: it is what makes a thermometer possible.
A thermometer is simply the third body C: its reading says whether two blocks would exchange heat.
Heat flows spontaneously from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.

slides.narration: Place a copper block and an aluminium block against the same thermometer. If both give the same reading, the zeroth law says the two blocks are in thermal equilibrium with each other, even though they never touched. Temperature is the property that is equal for bodies in thermal equilibrium, and the thermometer is the third body that lets us compare them.

slides.heading: Heat, work and internal energy
slides.body_md: Energy crosses the boundary of a system in two ways, and the system stores it as internal energy.
columns:
**Heat Q**
- Energy transferred by a temperature difference
- Flows in as the cup of tea cools
- Not "contained" in a body

**Work W**
- Energy transferred by a force moving its point of application
- A gas pushing a piston, a brake pad rubbing
- Also not stored in a body

Energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement
Energy of the random motion and mutual interaction of the molecules (centre of mass at rest)
No: it is energy in transit
No: it is energy in transit
No: only on the initial and final states

visual.alt: Table comparing heat, work and internal energy: what each is, whether it is a property of the system and whether it depends on the path

slides.narration: Heat is energy that moves because of a temperature difference. Work is energy that moves because a force acts through a displacement, for example a gas pushing a piston. Neither is stored in a body. What a body does store is internal energy, the energy of the random motion and the interactions of its molecules. That depends only on the state, not on how the state was reached.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: braking turns work into internal energy
slides.body_md: A 1200 kg car moving at 72 km h$^{-1}$ is brought to rest by its brakes. The brake assembly has a total heat capacity of $8$ kJ K$^{-1}$ and takes in all the energy. Find the rise in its temperature.
bullets: $v = 72$ km h$^{-1}$ $= 20$ m s$^{-1}$; kinetic energy $= \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 400 = 240000$ J.
Friction does work on the brakes; no heat flows in, yet the brakes warm up: their **internal energy rises**.
$\Delta T = \dfrac{\Delta U}{C} = \dfrac{240000}{8000} = 30$ K.

nodes.label: Friction does work on the brakes
Internal energy of the brakes rises

visual.alt: Flow diagram: kinetic energy of the car, friction work on the brakes, rise in the internal energy of the brakes
visual.caption: Work can change internal energy with no heat flow.

slides.narration: The car has kinetic energy of 240000 joules. Friction between pads and discs does work on the brakes, and no heat flows in at all, yet the brakes warm up. Their internal energy rises by 240000 joules. Divide by the heat capacity of eight thousand joules per kelvin and the temperature rise is 30 kelvin.

slides.heading: The first law of thermodynamics
slides.body_md: Energy is conserved. For a system: $\Delta U = Q - W$, where $W$ is the work done **by** the system.
bullets: Heat **added** to the system is positive; work done **by** the system is positive.
For compression, W is negative (work is done on the gas), so ΔU is larger than Q.
The first law ties together three energy changes; it does not say which way a process can go (that is the second law).
Some books write ΔU = Q + W with W as work done on the system; the physics is identical.

rows: heat flows out of the system
the gas expands and pushes on its surroundings
the gas is compressed: work is done on it
internal energy rises (an ideal gas warms up)
internal energy falls (an ideal gas cools)

visual.alt: Table of the sign convention used in the first law: heat into the system, work done by the system and change in internal energy

slides.narration: The first law is energy conservation. The change in internal energy equals the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system. We count heat into the system as positive and work done by the system as positive. When a gas is compressed, the work done by it is negative, so the internal energy rises by more than the heat added. Some books use the opposite sign for work, but the physics is the same.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: four cases of the first law
slides.body_md: For a gas, find ΔU in each case and say what happens to its temperature (take an ideal gas, so U rises with T).
bullets: Case 1: $Q = +500$ J, $W = +200$ J gives $\Delta U = 500 - (200) = +300$ J: heated while it pushes the piston out: warms up.
Case 2: $Q = -300$ J, $W = 0$ J gives $\Delta U = -300 - (0) = -300$ J: cooled in a rigid vessel: cools down.
Case 3: $Q = 0$ J, $W = -250$ J gives $\Delta U = 0 - (-250) = +250$ J: compressed in an insulated cylinder: warms up.
Case 4: $Q = +400$ J, $W = -100$ J gives $\Delta U = 400 - (-100) = +500$ J: heated while being compressed: warms up a lot.

rows: heated while it pushes the piston out: warms up
cooled in a rigid vessel: cools down
compressed in an insulated cylinder: warms up
heated while being compressed: warms up a lot

visual.alt: Table of four cases of heat and work for a gas with the change in internal energy worked out from the first law

slides.narration: Apply delta U equals Q minus W to each case. Heating the gas by five hundred joules while it does two hundred joules of work leaves three hundred joules in the gas. Cooling it by three hundred joules with no work removes three hundred. Compressing it with two hundred and fifty joules of work, and no heat flow, adds two hundred and fifty. Heating while compressing adds five hundred.

slides.heading: Work done by a gas: the area under the P–V graph
slides.body_md: When a gas pushes a piston of area $A$ through $dx$ at pressure $P$, the work is $P A\,dx = P\,dV$.
bullets: At **constant pressure**: $W = P(V_2 - V_1) = P\,\Delta V$.
In general W is the **area under the curve** on a P–V diagram: positive for expansion, negative for compression.
The area depends on the **path**, not just on the end points, so W is not a state function.
Unit bookkeeping: 1 kPa × 1 L = 1 J, because 10³ Pa × 10⁻³ m³ = 1 J.

slides.narration: The gas goes from two litres at three hundred kilopascals to five litres at two hundred kilopascals. The three areas give 900, 600 and 750 joules. The change in internal energy depends only on the end states, and comes to 600 joules. So the heat absorbed is 1500, 1200 and 1350 joules on the three paths. Work and heat depend on the path; internal energy does not.

slides.heading: Specific heat capacities of a gas
slides.body_md: A gas can be heated at constant volume or at constant pressure, and the heat needed for the same rise in temperature differs.
bullets: **Molar heat capacity at constant volume** $C_v$: $Q = n C_v \Delta T$ with $V$ fixed.
**Molar heat capacity at constant pressure** $C_p$: $Q = n C_p \Delta T$ with $P$ fixed.
At constant pressure the gas also does work P ΔV, so it needs more heat: **Cp is greater than Cv**.
Ratio $\gamma = C_p / C_v$; for a monatomic gas $C_v = \tfrac{3}{2}R$, for a diatomic gas $\tfrac{5}{2}R$ (values taken from kinetic theory, next chapter).

functions.label: constant pressure: Q = n Cp ΔT, slope 41.57 J/K
constant volume: Q = n Cv ΔT, slope 24.94 J/K

visual.alt: Graph of heat absorbed against temperature rise for 2 moles of a monatomic gas: the constant pressure line is steeper than the constant volume line, so more heat is needed at constant pressure for the same rise in temperature
visual.caption: The same ΔT needs more heat at constant pressure: the extra part is the work done by the gas.

slides.narration: The same temperature rise costs more heat at constant pressure than at constant volume, so the constant pressure line is steeper. At constant volume the gas does no work, so all the heat raises the internal energy. At constant pressure the gas also expands and does work, so it needs extra heat. The ratio of the two heat capacities is called gamma.

slides.heading: Why Cp − Cv = R
slides.body_md: Heat $n$ moles at constant pressure by $\Delta T$ and apply the first law.
bullets: ΔU for an ideal gas depends only on ΔT, so it is n Cv ΔT for any process between the same two temperatures.
The ideal gas law PV = nRT gives P ΔV = nR ΔT at constant pressure.
Numerically R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, so Cp is always 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ more than Cv.

rows: Diatomic (nitrogen, oxygen) at room temperature: Cv = 5R/2

visual.alt: Table of molar heat capacities at constant volume and constant pressure and the ratio gamma for monatomic and diatomic gases, using R equal to 8.314 joule per mole per kelvin

math: Q = n C_p \Delta T = \Delta U + P\,\Delta V
\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T, \qquad P\,\Delta V = n R\,\Delta T
slides.narration: Heat a gas at constant pressure. By the first law the heat equals the change in internal energy plus the work. For an ideal gas the change in internal energy is n times Cv times delta T. The work is pressure times change in volume, which the gas law turns into n R delta T. Dividing by n and delta T, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure minus that at constant volume equals R.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: heating a monatomic gas
slides.body_md: 2.0 mol of a monatomic ideal gas ($C_v = \tfrac{3}{2}R$, $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) is heated through $40$ K at constant pressure. Find the heat absorbed, the work done by the gas and the rise in internal energy.
bullets: $Q = nC_p\Delta T = 2.0 \times 20.79 \times 40 \approx 1663$ J.
$W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T = 2.0 \times 8.314 \times 40 \approx 665.1$ J.
$\Delta U = Q - W \approx 997.7$ J $= nC_v\Delta T$. The gas keeps $\dfrac{C_v}{C_p} = \dfrac{3}{5}$ of the heat; the rest does work.

rows: Diatomic (nitrogen, oxygen) at room temperature: Cv = 5R/2

visual.alt: Table of molar heat capacities at constant volume and constant pressure and the ratio gamma for monatomic and diatomic gases, using R equal to 8.314 joule per mole per kelvin

slides.narration: Take two moles of monatomic gas and heat it by forty kelvin at constant pressure. The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is five halves R, about 20.79 joules per mole per kelvin. The heat absorbed is about 1663 joules. The work done by the gas is n R delta T, about 665.1 joules. The rest, about 997.7 joules, raises the internal energy: three fifths of the heat.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Equilibrium with a third body means equilibrium with each other: temperature is well defined
Heat and work are energy in transit and path dependent; U is a state function
ΔU = Q − W (W done by the system)
W = ∫P dV = area under the P–V curve; W = PΔV at constant pressure
Q = nCvΔT (V constant), Q = nCpΔT (P constant); Cp − Cv = R

visual.alt: Summary table of the zeroth law, heat, work and internal energy, the first law, work as an area and the specific heats of a gas

slides.narration: To sum up. Temperature is defined by thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law. Heat and work are energy in transit and depend on the path, while internal energy is a property of the state. The first law says the change in internal energy is the heat added minus the work done by the system. Work is the area under the pressure volume curve. And the two molar heat capacities of a gas differ by R.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: State your sign convention for W before using ΔU = Q − W.
Never say a body "contains heat": heat is energy in transit; internal energy is what a body has.
For an area on a P–V graph, use kPa × L = J and check the sign from the direction of the volume change.
Write Cp − Cv = R with its derivation: first law at constant pressure plus PV = nRT.

rows: heat flows out of the system
the gas expands and pushes on its surroundings
the gas is compressed: work is done on it
internal energy rises (an ideal gas warms up)
internal energy falls (an ideal gas cools)

visual.alt: Table of the sign convention used in the first law: heat into the system, work done by the system and change in internal energy

slides.narration: State your sign convention before using the first law. Never say a body contains heat; say it has internal energy. When finding work from a graph, check the units and the direction of the volume change. And when asked for Cp minus Cv equals R, give the short derivation from the first law and the gas law.

slides.narration: A gas can be taken from one state to another in many ways. We can hold the temperature, the pressure or the volume fixed, or cut off all heat flow. In this part we meet those four basic processes, see how a cycle turns heat into work, and then learn the second law, which sets limits that the first law alone does not.

slides.heading: Quasi-static processes
slides.body_md: A **quasi-static** process is so slow that the system is in equilibrium at every stage.
bullets: The state variables P, V and T are defined at every instant, so the path can be drawn as a curve on a P–V diagram.
It is an idealisation: real processes are fast enough that the gas is briefly out of equilibrium.
Slow expansion with the pressure always equal to the outside pressure is quasi-static; a sudden burst is not.
We treat every P–V curve in this chapter as quasi-static; for a fast stroke this is an idealisation that assumes the gas stays uniform.

slides.narration: A quasi static process happens so slowly that the gas is in equilibrium at every stage. Only then do pressure, volume and temperature have definite values all along the way, and only then can we draw the path as a curve on a pressure volume diagram. Real processes are approximations to this ideal.

slides.heading: Isochoric and isobaric processes
slides.body_md: Keep the volume fixed, or keep the pressure fixed.
bullets: **Isochoric** (V constant): a vertical line on the P–V diagram, W = 0, so Q = ΔU = n Cv ΔT.
**Isobaric** (P constant): a horizontal line, W = P ΔV = n R ΔT, and Q = n Cp ΔT.
Heating a gas in a sealed rigid cylinder is isochoric; letting a gas push a free piston against steady atmospheric pressure is isobaric.
In both, ΔU = n Cv ΔT for an ideal gas.

rows: all the heat goes into internal energy
W = P ΔV = n R ΔT
part of the heat does the work P ΔV, the rest raises U

visual.alt: Table comparing an isochoric and an isobaric process: work done by the gas, heat absorbed and the reason

slides.narration: In an isochoric process the volume is fixed, so no work is done and all the heat raises the internal energy. In an isobaric process the pressure is fixed, so the work is pressure times the change in volume, and the heat is n times Cp times delta T. In both cases the change in internal energy of an ideal gas is n Cv delta T.

slides.heading: Isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
slides.body_md: Temperature constant: $PV = nRT$ = constant, a hyperbola on the P–V diagram.
bullets: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0.
The first law then gives **Q = W**: all the heat absorbed is turned into work.
This does not break the second law: the gas ends up at a larger volume, so this is not the sole result of a cycle.
It needs a reservoir at fixed temperature, and the process must be slow.

functions.label: isotherm through the adiabat's end (P V = 504 J)

visual.alt: P-V graph from a state at 2 litres and 400 kilopascals: an isotherm and a steeper adiabat that crosses to a lower isotherm, so the temperature falls during an adiabatic expansion
visual.caption: The adiabat crosses from one isotherm to a cooler one: expansion without heat input cools the gas.

slides.narration: In an isothermal process of an ideal gas the temperature does not change, so the pressure times the volume stays constant. The work is n R T times the natural logarithm of the volume ratio. Since the internal energy depends only on temperature, it does not change, so every joule of heat absorbed becomes work. That is allowed because the gas ends at a larger volume and nothing is cycled.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: isothermal expansion
slides.body_md: 0.50 mol of an ideal gas at $300$ K and $200$ kPa expands isothermally to 3 times its volume. Find the work done by the gas and the heat absorbed ($R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$).
bullets: $nRT = 0.50 \times 8.314 \times 300 \approx 1247$ J, so $V_1 = \dfrac{nRT}{P_1} \approx 6.24$ L and $V_2 = 3V_1 \approx 18.7$ L.
$W = nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = 1247 \times \ln 3 \approx 1370$ J.
$\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = W \approx 1370$ J absorbed from the surroundings.
Final pressure $P_2 = P_1/3 \approx 66.7$ kPa.

functions.label: isotherm at 300 K: P V = 1247 J

visual.alt: Isotherm at 300 kelvin for half a mole of ideal gas between 6.24 litres and 18.7 litres, with the area under the curve equal to the work done by the gas
visual.caption: The area under this curve between V₁ and V₂ is the work done by the gas.

slides.narration: For half a mole at three hundred kelvin, n R T is about 1247 joules. The gas expands to three times its volume, and the work is that number times the natural log of three, about 1370 joules. The internal energy is unchanged, so the gas absorbs the same 1370 joules as heat from the surroundings. The final pressure is a third of the initial one.

slides.heading: Adiabatic process: no heat in or out
slides.body_md: Q = 0, so $\Delta U = -W$. The gas follows $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.
bullets: Rapid processes and well-insulated ones are nearly adiabatic: a pump compressing air, sound waves, the sudden release of a gas.
Compression raises the temperature (work done on the gas goes into internal energy); expansion cools the gas.
On a P–V diagram the adiabat is **steeper** than the isotherm through the same point, by the factor γ.
So from the same state to the same final volume, an adiabatic expansion does **less work** than an isothermal one.

visual.alt: An isotherm and a steeper adiabat on a P-V diagram from the same starting state, with the area under each shaded
visual.caption: The adiabat is steeper and ends lower: less area, less work.

slides.narration: In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged, so the work done on the gas goes entirely into its internal energy. The gas obeys pressure times volume to the power gamma equals a constant. Compression heats it and expansion cools it. On the diagram the adiabat is steeper than the isotherm through the same point, so an adiabatic expansion between the same volumes does less work.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: compressing a gas adiabatically
slides.body_md: 1.0 mol of a monatomic ideal gas ($\gamma = \tfrac{5}{3}$, $C_v = \tfrac{3}{2}R$) at $300$ K and $100$ kPa is compressed adiabatically to half its volume. Find the final temperature, the final pressure and the work done by the gas.
bullets: $V_1 = \dfrac{nRT_1}{P_1} \approx 24.9$ L, $V_2 \approx 12.5$ L.
$T_2 = T_1\left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma - 1} = 300 \times 2^{2/3} \approx 476.2$ K.
$P_2 = P_1 \left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma} = 100 \times 2^{5/3} \approx 317.5$ kPa: **more than double** the starting pressure, because the gas also warms up.
$W = nC_v(T_1 - T_2) = 1.0 \times 12.47 \times (300 - 476.2) \approx -2198$ J. Negative: 2198 J of work is done **on** the gas, and $\Delta U = +2198$ J.

visual.alt: P-V graph for one mole of a monatomic gas compressed adiabatically from 24.9 litres to half that volume: the adiabat rises more steeply than the isotherm through the starting state
visual.caption: Compressed to half the volume, the pressure more than triples, not just doubles.

slides.narration: Compress one mole of monatomic gas to half its volume with no heat flow. The temperature rises as the volume ratio to the power two thirds, to about 476.2 kelvin. The pressure rises by the volume ratio to the power five thirds, about three point one eight times the starting pressure. The work done by the gas is about minus 2198 joules, so that much work was done on it, and its internal energy rises by the same amount.

slides.heading: Cyclic processes
slides.body_md: In a **cyclic process** the system returns to its initial state after a sequence of steps.
bullets: State variables return to their start values, so **ΔU = 0** over a full cycle and **Q = W** (net).
The net work is the **area enclosed** by the loop on the P–V diagram.
A **clockwise** loop gives positive net work (a heat engine); an **anticlockwise** loop gives negative net work (a refrigerator).
Heat is absorbed on some steps and rejected on others; net heat Q = Qin − Qout.

slides.narration: In a cyclic process the system comes back to its starting state. The internal energy therefore returns to its starting value, so the net heat equals the net work. On a pressure volume diagram the net work is the enclosed area. Run the loop clockwise and the net work is positive, as in an engine. Run it anticlockwise and the net work is negative, as in a refrigerator.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a rectangular cycle as an engine
slides.body_md: A monatomic ideal gas ($C_v = \tfrac{3}{2}R$) is taken round the cycle A→B→C→D→A of the figure. Find the net work, the heat absorbed, the heat rejected and the efficiency of this engine.
bullets: AB (isochoric, heating): $Q = \tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(PV) = \tfrac{3}{2}(600 - 200) = 600$ J. BC (isobaric, expansion): $Q = \tfrac{5}{2}P\Delta V = \tfrac{5}{2} \times 300 \times 4 = 3000$ J.
Heat absorbed $Q_1 = 600 + 3000 = 3600$ J.
CD: $Q = -1800$ J; DA: $Q = -1000$ J, so heat rejected $Q_2 = 2800$ J. Check: $Q_1 - Q_2 = 800 = W$.
Efficiency $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_1} = \dfrac{800}{3600} \approx 22.2\%$.

slides.narration: The net work is the area of the rectangle, 800 joules. Heat is absorbed on the heating step at constant volume, 600 joules, and on the expansion at constant pressure, 3000 joules, a total of 3600 joules. The other two steps reject 2800 joules. The difference is the work, as it must be, and the efficiency is work over heat absorbed, about 22.2 percent.

slides.heading: The second law: two statements
slides.body_md: The first law only counts energy. It allows a stone to cool the ground and jump up; nature never does this. The **second law** gives the direction.
bullets: **Kelvin–Planck:** no cyclic device can take heat from a single reservoir and convert **all** of it into work with no other effect.
**Clausius:** no cyclic device can have, as its only result, the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter one.
The two are equivalent: breaking one lets you break the other.
Result: every engine rejects some heat, and every refrigerator needs work.

rows: A cyclic device taking heat from one reservoir and converting all of it into work, with no other effect
Some heat must always be rejected: no engine is 100% efficient
A cyclic device whose only result is to move heat from a colder body to a hotter one
A refrigerator needs work: heat does not flow uphill by itself

visual.alt: Table of the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements of the second law of thermodynamics and what each forbids

slides.narration: The first law says energy is conserved but does not forbid a stone from cooling the ground and leaping into the air. The second law rules such things out. The Kelvin Planck statement says no cyclic device can turn all the heat from one reservoir into work. The Clausius statement says heat cannot flow from cold to hot as the only result. The two statements are equivalent.

slides.heading: Reversible and irreversible processes
slides.body_md: A process is **reversible** if it can be retraced exactly, leaving no change in the system or its surroundings.
bullets: It must be quasi-static and free of friction, turbulence and heat flow across a finite temperature difference.
Almost every natural process is **irreversible**: free expansion, friction, heat flow across a gap, mixing, dissolving.
Reversible processes are ideal limits that real processes only approach.
The second law says irreversible processes are one-way: a cup of coffee cools, but never heats itself from the room.

rows: A gas rushes into an evacuated chamber
The gas never collects itself back into one chamber
Heat flows from a hot spoon to cold tea
Heat flow across a finite temperature gap is one-way
A sliding block is stopped by friction
Work turns into heat that cannot turn fully back into work
A gas expands very slowly, with no friction, in contact with a reservoir
Every stage is in equilibrium; a tiny change reverses it

visual.alt: Table of four processes labelled reversible or irreversible, each with the reason

slides.narration: A reversible process can be retraced exactly. That needs it to be quasi static and free of friction and of heat flow across a finite temperature difference. Real processes such as free expansion, friction, mixing and heat flowing from hot to cold are irreversible. Reversible processes are ideal limits that we approach but never quite reach.

slides.heading: Heat engines and refrigerators
slides.body_md: An **engine** takes heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir, converts part to work W and rejects Q₂ to a cold reservoir. A **refrigerator** runs the other way.
bullets: Cyclic operation: ΔU = 0, so W = Q₁ − Q₂ for both devices.
Efficiency η is always below 1 (Kelvin–Planck); the coefficient of performance COP can be above 1.
A refrigerator hands the kitchen more heat (Q₁) than it removes from the food (Q₂): Q₁ = Q₂ + W.

slides.narration: To sum up. In an isochoric process no work is done. In an isobaric process the work is pressure times the change in volume. sections.heading: 1. Thermal equilibrium, the zeroth law, heat, work and internal energy
sections.body_md:
- A **system** is the part of the world under study; the rest is its **surroundings**. Two systems in contact are in **thermal equilibrium** when no net heat flows between them. An **adiabatic wall** stops heat; a **diathermic wall** lets it pass.
- **Zeroth law:** if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body C, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. **Temperature** is the property that is equal for systems in thermal equilibrium; a thermometer is the third body.
- **Heat** is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; **work** is energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement. Neither is "contained" in a body: they are energy in transit and depend on the path.
- **Internal energy** $U$ is the energy of the random motion and mutual interaction of the molecules, measured with the centre of mass at rest. It is a **state function**: it depends only on the state of the system.
- Work can raise internal energy with no heat flow: a 1200 kg car stopped from 72 km h⁻¹ puts 240000 J into brakes of heat capacity 8 kJ K⁻¹ and warms them by 30 K.

key_terms.definition_md: The state in which no net heat flows between two systems in contact: they have the same temperature.

sections.heading: 2. First law, work done by a gas and specific heats
sections.body_md:
- **First law:** $\Delta U = Q - W$. $Q$ is positive when heat flows **into** the system; $W$ is the work done **by** the system (positive for expansion, negative for compression). Books that use $W$ for work done on the system write $\Delta U = Q + W$; the physics is the same.
- **Work by a gas:** $W = \int P\,dV$ is the **area under the P–V curve**; at constant pressure $W = P\,\Delta V$. With $P$ in kPa and $V$ in litres the area is in joules (1 kPa × 1 L = 1 J). The work depends on the **path**: for one state-to-state change (A to B in a figure of 2 L, 300 kPa to 5 L, 200 kPa) three paths give 900 J, 600 J and 750 J, while $\Delta U$ is the same 600 J, so $Q$ is 1500 J, 1200 J and 1350 J.
- **Specific heats of a gas:** $Q = nC_v\Delta T$ at constant volume and $Q = nC_p\Delta T$ at constant pressure. For an ideal gas $\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$ for every process. At constant pressure the gas also does work $nR\,\Delta T$, so $C_p - C_v = R = 8.314$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and $\gamma = C_p/C_v$.
- Example: 2.0 mol of a monatomic gas heated by 40 K at constant pressure takes in 1663 J: 665.1 J is work and 997.7 J raises the internal energy. Data from kinetic theory (next chapter): $C_v = 3R/2$ for a monatomic and $5R/2$ for a diatomic gas.

key_terms.definition_md: ΔU = Q − W: the heat added to a system minus the work done by it equals the increase in its internal energy.
Heat per mole per kelvin: Cv at constant volume, Cp at constant pressure.
A quantity fixed by the state of the system (U, P, V, T), not by the path taken.

sections.heading: 3. Thermodynamic processes
sections.body_md:
- A **quasi-static** process is so slow that the system is in equilibrium at every stage, so it can be drawn as a curve on a P–V diagram.
- **Isochoric** ($V$ constant): $W = 0$, $Q = \Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$. **Isobaric** ($P$ constant): $W = P\,\Delta V = nR\,\Delta T$, $Q = nC_p\Delta T$.
- **Isothermal** ideal gas ($T$ constant, $PV$ constant): $\Delta U = 0$, $Q = W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$. For 0.50 mol at 300 K expanding to 3 times its volume, $W = Q \approx 1370$ J.
- **Adiabatic** ($Q = 0$): $\Delta U = -W$, $PV^{\gamma} = $ constant, $TV^{\gamma-1} = $ constant, $W = (P_1V_1 - P_2V_2)/(\gamma - 1) = nC_v(T_1 - T_2)$. The adiabat is steeper than the isotherm through the same point (by the factor $\gamma$), so an adiabatic expansion between the same volumes does less work. Compressing 1.0 mol of a monatomic gas from 300 K to half its volume heats it to 476.2 K and needs 2198 J of work.
- **Cyclic:** the system returns to its start, so $\Delta U = 0$ and the net work equals the net heat; the net work is the **area enclosed** by the loop, positive if the loop is run clockwise (engine). The rectangular cycle of the figure encloses 800 J; it absorbs 3600 J and rejects 2800 J (efficiency 22.2%).

sections.heading: 4. The second law, reversibility, heat engines and refrigerators
sections.body_md:
- **Kelvin–Planck statement:** no cyclic device can absorb heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work with no other effect. **Clausius statement:** no cyclic device can have as its only result the transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter body. They are equivalent. The first law cannot rule such processes out; the second law does.
- A process is **reversible** only if it is quasi-static and free of friction and of heat flow across a finite temperature difference; free expansion, friction, mixing and conduction across a gap are **irreversible**.
- A **heat engine** takes $Q_1$ from a hot reservoir, delivers $W$ and rejects $Q_2$; $W = Q_1 - Q_2$ and the **efficiency** is $\eta = W/Q_1 = 1 - Q_2/Q_1$, always less than 1. An engine absorbing 5 kJ and rejecting 3.8 kJ has $\eta = 24.0\%$.
- A **refrigerator** takes $Q_2$ from the cold space with work $W$ and releases $Q_1 = Q_2 + W$; its **coefficient of performance** is $\text{COP} = Q_2/W = Q_2/(Q_1 - Q_2)$, which can exceed 1. One removing 1.8 MJ per hour for 0.45 MJ of work has COP 4 and releases 2.25 MJ to the room.
- The Carnot engine and Carnot's theorem are not covered here (see README).

key_terms.definition_md: A cyclic device that converts part of the heat absorbed from a hot reservoir into work and rejects the rest to a cold reservoir.
For a refrigerator, the heat removed from the cold space divided by the work supplied.
A process that cannot be retraced exactly; natural processes with friction, free expansion or heat flow across a gap.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Write the sign convention (W done by the gas) before using ΔU = Q − W.
- Heat and work are energy in transit; only internal energy belongs to a body.
- Work from a graph: area under the P–V curve (kPa × L = J), positive if V increases.
- Isothermal: ΔU = 0, Q = W. Adiabatic: Q = 0, ΔU = −W, PV^γ = constant.
- Efficiency η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ is always less than 1; COP = Q₂/W can exceed 1.

cards.front_md: What does the zeroth law of thermodynamics say?
cards.back_md: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

cards.front_md: What property do two systems in thermal equilibrium share?
cards.back_md: The same temperature.

cards.front_md: How does an adiabatic wall differ from a diathermic wall?
cards.back_md: An adiabatic wall blocks heat flow; a diathermic wall lets heat pass.

cards.front_md: Define heat.
cards.back_md: Energy transferred between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference.

cards.front_md: Why is "heat content of a body" a wrong phrase?
cards.back_md: Heat is energy in transit, not a stored property; the body has internal energy.

cards.front_md: What is internal energy?
cards.back_md: The energy of the random motion and mutual interaction of the molecules (centre of mass at rest); a state function.

cards.front_md: Name two ways to raise the internal energy of a gas.
cards.back_md: Add heat, or do work on it (for example compress it).

cards.front_md: Which of Q, W and ΔU depend only on the initial and final states?
cards.back_md: Only ΔU; Q and W depend on the path.

cards.front_md: State the first law with its sign convention.
cards.back_md: ΔU = Q − W: Q positive into the system, W positive for work done by the system.

cards.front_md: A gas takes in 500 J and does 200 J of work. ΔU?
Work done by a gas at constant pressure?
cards.back_md: W = PΔV = P(V₂ − V₁).

cards.front_md: General expression for work done by a gas?
cards.back_md: W = ∫P dV, the area under the P–V curve.

cards.front_md: What is 1 kPa × 1 L in joules?
Is the work done by a gas negative or positive in compression?
cards.back_md: Negative (work is done on the gas).

cards.front_md: Same end states, different paths: what is the same and what differs?
cards.back_md: ΔU is the same; W and Q differ.

cards.front_md: Which is larger for a gas, Cp or Cv, and why?
cards.back_md: Cp: at constant pressure the gas also does work PΔV.

cards.front_md: Relation between Cp and Cv for an ideal gas?
cards.back_md: Cp − Cv = R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Value of Cp for a monatomic gas (Cv = 3R/2)?
What is a quasi-static process?
cards.back_md: A process so slow that the system is in equilibrium at every stage.

cards.front_md: In an isochoric process what is W and what is Q?
cards.back_md: W = 0; Q = ΔU = nCvΔT.

cards.front_md: Work and heat in an isobaric process?
cards.back_md: W = PΔV = nRΔT; Q = nCpΔT.

cards.front_md: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, what is ΔU and what is Q?
cards.back_md: ΔU = 0; Q = W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).

cards.front_md: What condition defines an adiabatic process, and what follows for ΔU?
cards.back_md: Q = 0, so ΔU = −W.

cards.front_md: Adiabatic relations for an ideal gas?
cards.back_md: PV^γ = constant and TV^(γ−1) = constant.

cards.front_md: Which is steeper on a P–V diagram, an adiabat or an isotherm?
cards.back_md: The adiabat (by the factor γ at the same point).

cards.front_md: In a cyclic process what are ΔU and the net work?
cards.back_md: ΔU = 0; net work = area of the loop (positive if clockwise) = net heat.

cards.front_md: State the Kelvin–Planck statement.
cards.back_md: No cyclic device can convert all the heat from a single reservoir into work with no other effect.

cards.front_md: State the Clausius statement.
cards.back_md: No cyclic device can have, as its only result, heat flowing from a colder to a hotter body.

cards.front_md: Give two examples of irreversible processes.
cards.back_md: Free expansion into a vacuum; friction; heat flow across a finite temperature gap.

cards.front_md: Formulas for efficiency and coefficient of performance?
cards.back_md: η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ (always < 1); COP = Q₂/W (can exceed 1).

questions.stem_md: In a school laboratory a steel ball and a brass cylinder are pressed, one after the other, against the bulb of the same mercury thermometer, and each time it reads 35 °C. Without bringing the two bodies together, the teacher says they would show no net heat flow if they were placed in contact. This conclusion rests on

options.text_md: the first law of thermodynamics
the Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law
the zeroth law of thermodynamics
Newton’s law of cooling

questions.solution_md: Both bodies are in thermal equilibrium with the thermometer, so they are in thermal equilibrium with each other: this is the zeroth law — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A red-hot copper rod is dropped into a bucket of water and the water warms up. Which description is physically correct?

options.text_md: Energy passes from the rod to the water because of the temperature difference; the energy transferred in this way is called heat
The rod contained a store of heat, which has now been poured into the water
The rod has done work on the water, since the temperature of the water has changed
The internal energy of the rod has risen while that of the water has fallen

questions.solution_md: Heat is energy in transit driven by a temperature difference; it is not a stored quantity. The rod’s internal energy falls and the water’s rises — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A fixed mass of gas is taken from state X to state Y by two different routes. Which quantity must have the same value on both routes?

options.text_md: the heat absorbed by the gas
the change in the internal energy of the gas
the work done by the gas
the sum of the heat absorbed and the work done by the gas

questions.solution_md: Internal energy is a state function, so ΔU depends only on X and Y. Q and W depend on the route. Because ΔU = Q − W, the sum Q + W also changes with the route — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The total energy of the random motion and the mutual interaction of all the molecules of the gas in a closed cylinder, measured with the cylinder’s centre of mass at rest, is called the ___ energy of the gas.
questions.solution_md: It is the **internal** energy of the gas, a function of its state.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A hot iron spoon contains more heat than an identical cold spoon, which is why heat is described as a property stored in the spoon.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference. The hot spoon has more internal energy, but "heat" is the name of the transfer, not of a stored quantity.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** With a thermometer, a student can say whether two bodies would exchange heat without bringing the bodies into contact.

**Reason (R):** The kelvin is the SI unit of temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. A follows from the zeroth law (equal readings mean equal temperatures), but the choice of unit does not explain it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A city bus of mass 9000 kg slows from 36 km/h to rest on a level road. Its brake assembly absorbs all the kinetic energy and has a total heat capacity of 120 kJ/K. Find the rise in the temperature of the brakes, in K.
questions.solution_md: $v = 36$ km/h $= 10$ m/s, so the kinetic energy given to the brakes is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9000 \times 100 = 450000$ J. Then $\Delta T = \dfrac{450000}{120000} = 3.75$ K.

questions.stem_md: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain how it makes a thermometer a meaningful instrument.

answer.model_answer_md: The **zeroth law**: if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. The thermometer is the third body: equal readings on two bodies mean equal temperatures, so the bodies would exchange no net heat if put in contact.

questions.solution_md: Statement of the law; thermometer as the third body.

marking_scheme.step: Statement: A and B each in equilibrium with C ⇒ A and B in equilibrium
Thermometer is the third body: equal readings mean equal temperature, no net heat flow

questions.stem_md: Distinguish an adiabatic wall from a diathermic wall, and say what happens to the temperatures of two systems separated by each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **adiabatic wall** does not let heat pass: two systems separated by it keep their own temperatures, even if these differ. A **diathermic wall** lets heat pass: two systems separated by it exchange heat until they reach one common temperature, that is, thermal equilibrium.

questions.solution_md: Adiabatic blocks heat; diathermic allows it, ending in equilibrium.

marking_scheme.step: Adiabatic wall blocks heat; the systems keep different temperatures
Diathermic wall allows heat flow until the temperatures become equal

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between heat, work and internal energy of a gas, and say which of the three depend on the path by which the gas goes from one state to another.

answer.model_answer_md: **Heat** is energy transferred between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference; **work** is energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement, as when a gas pushes a piston. Both are energy in transit. **Internal energy** is the energy of the molecules, a property of the state. Heat and work depend on the path; internal energy does not.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; heat and work are path dependent; U is a state function.

marking_scheme.step: Heat: energy transfer due to temperature difference
Work: transfer by a force through a displacement; internal energy: molecular energy of the state
Q and W are path dependent; U depends only on the state

questions.stem_md: A gas in a cylinder is compressed so that 150 J of work is done on it, while it loses 40 J of heat to the surroundings. The change in the internal energy of the gas is
questions.solution_md: Heat into the gas $Q = -40$ J; work done by the gas $W = -150$ J. $\Delta U = Q - W = -40 - (-150) = +110$ J — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A gas in a cylinder absorbs 640 J of heat and does 260 J of work in pushing the piston out. Find the increase in the internal energy of the gas, in J.
A gas in a cylinder with a free piston pushes it out at a steady pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa while its volume grows from 4.0 L to 9.0 L. Find the work done by the gas, in J.
On a P–V diagram a gas goes from (1.5 L, 400 kPa) to (4.5 L, 150 kPa) along a straight line. Find the work done by the gas, in J.
questions.solution_md: Work = area under the line = trapezoid $= \tfrac{1}{2}(400 + 150) \times (4.5 - 1.5) = 825$ J (kPa × L = J).

marking_scheme.step: Area under the straight line is a trapezoid

questions.stem_md: A gas is taken from state A to state B by path 1, absorbing 900 J of heat and doing 500 J of work. By path 2, between the same two states, it does 300 J of work. Find the heat it absorbs along path 2, in J.
questions.solution_md: Internal energy is a state function: $\Delta U = Q_1 - W_1 = 900 - 500 = 400$ J on either path. Path 2: $Q_2 = \Delta U + W_2 = 400 + 300 = 700$ J.

marking_scheme.step: ΔU = 900 − 500 = 400 J, the same on both paths

questions.stem_md: A gas has γ = Cp/Cv = 1.40. Using Cp − Cv = R with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find Cv in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $C_p = \gamma C_v$, so $(\gamma - 1)C_v = R$ and $C_v = \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{8.314}{0.40} = 20.8$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

marking_scheme.step: Cp = γCv and Cp − Cv = R give (γ − 1)Cv = R

questions.stem_md: A monatomic ideal gas has Cv = 3R/2 with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the heat needed to raise the temperature of 3.0 mol of it by 30 K at constant pressure, in J (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $C_p = C_v + R = \tfrac{3}{2}R + R = \tfrac{5}{2}R = 20.785$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. $Q = nC_p\Delta T = 3 \times 20.785 \times 30 = 1871$ J, that is about 1870 J.

questions.stem_md: More heat is needed to warm a sample of gas by 10 K at constant pressure than at constant volume. The reason is that at constant pressure

options.text_md: the gas contains more molecules than at constant volume
the internal energy of an ideal gas rises more for the same temperature change
the gas expands and does work on its surroundings, so extra heat is needed beyond what raises its internal energy
heat is lost to the cylinder walls only when the volume is held fixed

questions.solution_md: For an ideal gas $\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$ is the same in both cases; at constant pressure the gas also does work $P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$, so $C_p = C_v + R$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: On a P–V diagram a gas is compressed at a steady 200 kPa from 6.0 L to 2.0 L. The work done by the gas is
questions.solution_md: $W = P\,\Delta V = 200 \times (2.0 - 6.0) = -800$ J (kPa × L = J). The negative sign shows that work is done on the gas — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a gas in a sealed rigid cylinder is heated, all the heat supplied goes into raising its internal energy.

**Reason (R):** A gas whose volume does not change does no work on its surroundings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true (W = P ΔV = 0 when ΔV = 0), and with W = 0 the first law gives Q = ΔU, which is A. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State the first law of thermodynamics with the sign convention you use, and say which general principle of physics it expresses.

answer.model_answer_md: The heat **Q** supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy **ΔU** plus the work **W** done by it: ΔU = Q − W. Heat into the system and work done by the system are taken as positive. It expresses the **conservation of energy**, with heat counted as a form of energy transfer.

questions.solution_md: ΔU = Q − W with signs; conservation of energy.

marking_scheme.step: ΔU = Q − W; Q positive into the system, W positive when done by it

questions.stem_md: Explain why the molar heat capacity of an ideal gas at constant pressure is larger than at constant volume, and write the relation between the two.

answer.model_answer_md: At constant volume the gas does no work, so all the heat raises its internal energy. At constant pressure the gas also expands and does work **PΔV = nRΔT**, so more heat is needed for the same rise in temperature. Hence **Cp − Cv = R**.

questions.solution_md: Extra work at constant pressure; Cp − Cv = R.

marking_scheme.step: Constant volume: no work; constant pressure: the gas also does work PΔV

questions.stem_md: Using the first law of thermodynamics, derive the relation Cp − Cv = R for one mole of an ideal gas.

answer.model_answer_md: Heat one mole of the gas at constant pressure through a temperature rise $\Delta T$. By the first law the heat supplied goes partly into internal energy and partly into the work done by the gas: $C_p\Delta T = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For an ideal gas the internal energy change is $\Delta U = C_v\Delta T$ whatever the process, and the gas law $PV = RT$ at constant pressure gives $P\Delta V = R\Delta T$. Substituting, $C_p\Delta T = C_v\Delta T + R\Delta T$, hence $C_p - C_v = R$.

questions.solution_md: First law at constant pressure; ΔU = CvΔT; PΔV = RΔT.

marking_scheme.step: First law at constant pressure: CpΔT = ΔU + PΔV
ΔU = CvΔT and PΔV = RΔT (from PV = RT)

questions.stem_md: Two students take the same gas from state A to state B, one along a straight line on the P–V diagram and the other along a curve lying below it. Explain, with the first law, why they find the same ΔU but different values of Q, and say which student’s gas absorbs less heat.

answer.model_answer_md: Internal energy is a state function, so $\Delta U$ depends only on A and B and is the same for both. Work is the area under the path, which is smaller for the curve below the line, so $W$ is smaller. Since $Q = \Delta U + W$, the heat absorbed also differs, and the student on the lower curve has the smaller $Q$.

questions.solution_md: ΔU same; W is the area under the path; Q = ΔU + W is smaller for the smaller area.

marking_scheme.step: Work is the area under the path: smaller for the lower curve
Q = ΔU + W: the lower curve needs less heat

questions.stem_md: On the P–V diagram of a gas, a process is drawn as a vertical straight line running downwards. The process is

options.text_md: an isobaric compression, since the pressure changes
an isothermal expansion, since the line is straight
an adiabatic expansion, since no volume change takes place
an isochoric one in which the pressure falls: no work is done and heat flows out of the gas

questions.solution_md: A vertical line has $\Delta V = 0$, so $W = \int P\,dV = 0$ and $Q = \Delta U$. The pressure (and for an ideal gas the temperature) falls, so $\Delta U < 0$ and heat leaves the gas — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An ideal gas expands from the same initial state to the same final volume, once isothermally and once adiabatically. Which statement about the final states is correct?

options.text_md: Both final pressures are equal, because the final volume is the same
The final pressure is lower in the adiabatic case, because the gas also cools down
The final pressure is lower in the isothermal case, because it absorbs heat
The final pressure is higher in the adiabatic case, because no heat escapes

questions.solution_md: Isothermal: $P_2 = P_1V_1/V_2$. Adiabatic: $P_2 = P_1(V_1/V_2)^{\gamma}$ with $\gamma > 1$, which is smaller. The gas does work at the cost of its internal energy and cools — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A cyclist inflates a tyre with a hand pump, working vigorously, and finds that the lower end of the pump barrel becomes warm. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: the air is compressed so quickly that little heat escapes, so the work done on it raises its internal energy and temperature
heat flows into the air from the cyclist’s warm hand
the pressure of the air rises, and by Boyle’s law that alone raises its temperature
compressing a gas never changes its temperature; only friction in the barrel does

questions.solution_md: A fast compression is nearly adiabatic: $Q \approx 0$, so $\Delta U = -W > 0$ because $W$ (done by the gas) is negative. The air’s temperature rises — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Removing a partition lets an ideal gas rush from one half of an insulated, rigid box into the empty other half (free expansion). The temperature of the gas

options.text_md: falls, because the gas expands
rises, because the pressure drops suddenly
does not change, because Q = 0 and W = 0, so ΔU = 0
falls, because the gas does work against the empty half

questions.solution_md: The box is insulated ($Q = 0$) and rigid with nothing to push against ($W = 0$), so $\Delta U = 0$. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so $T$ is unchanged — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A gas goes round a closed loop on a P–V diagram in the anticlockwise direction. For one complete loop

options.text_md: net work is done by the gas, and an equal net amount of heat enters the gas
the net work is zero, because the gas returns to its initial state
the internal energy of the gas decreases by an amount equal to the area of the loop
net work is done on the gas, and an equal net amount of heat leaves the gas

questions.solution_md: After a full loop $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q_\text{net} = W_\text{net}$. An anticlockwise loop has negative net work by the gas (work is done on it), so the net heat is negative: heat leaves — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the work done by the gas comes from a decrease in its internal energy.

**Reason (R):** During an isothermal expansion, the gas absorbs from its surroundings an amount of heat equal to the work it does.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: Q = W. A is false: for an ideal gas ΔU = 0 at constant temperature, so the work does not come from the internal energy — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When an ideal gas is compressed adiabatically, the work done on it appears entirely as an increase in its internal energy.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. With Q = 0 the first law gives ΔU = −W, and W (done by the gas) is negative in compression, so ΔU is positive.

questions.stem_md: A student seals a syringe, wraps it in thick foam so that no heat can pass in or out, and pushes the plunger in quickly. A process in which Q = 0 is called an ___ process.
questions.solution_md: A process with no heat exchange is **adiabatic**; here ΔU = −W.

questions.stem_md: Match each thermodynamic process of a gas in Column A with what the first law says about it in Column B.

options.text_md: Isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
Adiabatic compression of a gas
Heating a gas in a sealed rigid cylinder
Heating a gas under a freely moving piston at steady pressure

match_right.text_md: No heat enters or leaves, so ΔU = −W
No work is done, so Q = ΔU

questions.solution_md: Isothermal: ΔU = 0 so Q = W (r). Adiabatic: Q = 0 so ΔU = −W (p). Rigid cylinder (isochoric): W = 0 so Q = ΔU (q). Steady pressure (isobaric): W = PΔV and Q = nCpΔT (s).

questions.stem_md: A sample of 0.80 mol of an ideal gas at 320 K expands isothermally until its volume is 2.5 times the initial volume. Take R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the work done by the gas, in J (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $W = nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = 0.8 \times 8.314 \times 320 \times \ln 2.5 = 2128.4 \times 0.9163$ J, so $W = 1950$ J.

questions.stem_md: Air (treated as an ideal gas with γ = 1.40) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. Find its final temperature, in K (3 significant figures).
One mole of a monatomic ideal gas (Cv = 3R/2, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 400 K expands adiabatically until its temperature is 300 K. Find the work done by the gas, in J (nearest joule).
questions.solution_md: $Q = 0$, so $W = -\Delta U = nC_v(T_1 - T_2) = 1 \times \tfrac{3}{2} \times 8.314 \times (400 - 300) = 1247$ J, so $W = 1247$ J.

questions.stem_md: Air in a pump (0.50 mol, treated as a diatomic ideal gas with Cv = 5R/2 and γ = 1.40) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-quarter of its volume. Find the work done on the gas, in J (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $T_2 = T_1 \times 4^{0.40} = 300 \times 1.741 = 522.3$ K. Work done on the gas $= \Delta U = nC_v(T_2 - T_1) = 0.5 \times 20.785 \times 222.3 = 2311$ J, so $W_\text{on} = 2310$ J.

marking_scheme.step: Q = 0: work done on the gas = ΔU = nCvΔT

questions.stem_md: Air (γ = 1.40) at 100 kPa is compressed adiabatically to one-fifth of its volume. Find the final pressure, in kPa (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $P_1V_1^{\gamma} = P_2V_2^{\gamma}$, so $P_2 = P_1\left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma} = 100 \times 5^{1.40} = 100 \times 9.518$ kPa, so $P_2 = 952$ kPa.

questions.stem_md: A gas is taken round the triangular loop A → B → C → A on a P–V diagram, with A (1.0 L, 100 kPa), B (1.0 L, 250 kPa) and C (4.0 L, 100 kPa), A to B being vertical and C to A horizontal. Find the net work done by the gas in one loop, in J.
questions.solution_md: The net work is the area of the triangle: base $= (4.0 - 1.0)$ L $= 3.0$ L, height $= (250 - 100)$ kPa $= 150$ kPa. Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3.0 \times 150 = 225$ J. The loop A→B→C→A runs clockwise, so the net work done by the gas is positive: $W = +225$ J.

marking_scheme.step: Net work = area enclosed: ½ × base × height
½ × 3.0 × 150 = 225 J, positive for a clockwise loop

questions.stem_md: A diatomic gas (Cv = 5R/2, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) in a sealed rigid cylinder, 2.0 mol, is heated through 25 K. Find the heat absorbed, in J (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The volume is fixed, so $W = 0$ and $Q = \Delta U = nC_v\Delta T = 2 \times \tfrac{5}{2} \times 8.314 \times 25 = 1039$ J, so $Q = 1040$ J.

marking_scheme.step: V constant: W = 0, so Q = nCvΔT

questions.stem_md: A sample of 0.25 mol of an ideal gas at 350 K is compressed isothermally to one-third of its volume (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Find the heat given out by the gas to its surroundings, in J (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = W = nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = 0.25 \times 8.314 \times 350 \times \ln\dfrac{1}{3} = 727.48 \times (-1.099) = -799.2$ J. The negative sign means heat leaves the gas, so the heat given out is $-Q = 799$ J.

marking_scheme.step: ΔU = 0, so Q = W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)
ln(1/3) = −1.099; Q = −799.2 J, so heat given out = 799 J

questions.stem_md: At state B of a cycle, 0.20 mol of an ideal gas has pressure 300 kPa and volume 4.0 L. Using PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find its temperature at B, in K (3 significant figures).
What is meant by a quasi-static process? Why can the expansion of a gas be drawn as a curve on a P–V diagram only if it is quasi-static?

answer.model_answer_md: A **quasi-static** process is carried out so slowly that the system is in thermal and mechanical equilibrium at every stage. Only then do P, V and T have single, definite values at each instant, so each intermediate state is a point and the whole path can be drawn as a curve on a P–V diagram.

questions.solution_md: Equilibrium at each stage; definite P, V, T give points on the curve.

marking_scheme.step: Quasi-static: so slow that the system is in equilibrium at every stage
Only then are P, V and T defined at each instant, giving a curve of points

questions.stem_md: A gas goes through a complete cycle and returns to its initial state. State, with reasons, the change in its internal energy and the relation between the net heat absorbed and the net work done.

answer.model_answer_md: Internal energy is a state function, so after a full cycle $\Delta U = 0$. The first law then gives $Q_\text{net} = W_\text{net}$: the net heat absorbed by the gas in the cycle equals the net work it does, which is the area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram.

questions.solution_md: ΔU = 0, so Q = W.

marking_scheme.step: ΔU = 0 over a cycle because U is a state function
First law: net heat = net work (area of the loop)

questions.stem_md: An ideal gas expands from the same initial state to the same final volume, once isothermally and once adiabatically. Compare (a) the final temperatures and (b) the work done, giving a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Isothermally the temperature stays the same. Adiabatically $Q = 0$, the gas does work at the cost of its internal energy and cools, so its final temperature is lower. (b) The adiabat is steeper than the isotherm on the P–V diagram, so the area under it is smaller: the gas does less work in the adiabatic expansion.

questions.solution_md: Final T lower for adiabat; steeper curve, smaller area, less work.

marking_scheme.step: Isothermal: T unchanged; adiabatic: Q = 0 and the gas cools
Adiabat is steeper than the isotherm through the same point
Smaller area under the adiabat: less work done

questions.stem_md: An inventor displays a machine that, working in a cycle, draws 800 J of heat from a boiler and turns all of it into 800 J of work, with no heat rejected anywhere. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: It violates the first law, because energy would not be conserved
It violates the second law (Kelvin–Planck statement), although it does not violate energy conservation
It violates the zeroth law, because the boiler and the machine are not in equilibrium
It violates no law; it is simply a very efficient engine

questions.solution_md: Energy is conserved (800 J in, 800 J out), so the first law is satisfied. But converting all the heat from one reservoir into work in a cycle is forbidden by the Kelvin–Planck statement — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A box with no power supply and no moving parts is claimed to keep its inside at 5 °C while standing in a room at 30 °C, simply by moving heat out of its interior. This claim would break

options.text_md: the Kelvin–Planck statement alone, but not the Clausius statement
the first law, because heat cannot be conserved
the zeroth law, because the box and the room are not in thermal equilibrium
the Clausius statement of the second law

questions.solution_md: Heat would flow from a colder region to a hotter one with no work input and no other effect, which the Clausius statement rules out — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Four inventors report data for engines working in cycles: heat absorbed Q₁, work done W and heat rejected Q₂ per cycle, all in J. Which set can be consistent with both the first and the second law?
questions.solution_md: Over a cycle W = Q₁ − Q₂ (first law), and Q₂ must be greater than 0 (second law). Q₁ = 800, W = 300, Q₂ = 500 gives 800 − 500 = 300 with Q₂ > 0: allowed. The set Q₁ = 600, W = 600, Q₂ = 0 has Q₂ = 0 (violates the second law); Q₁ = 500, W = 200, Q₂ = 400 has 500 − 400 = 100 ≠ 200 and Q₁ = 700, W = 250, Q₂ = 400 has 700 − 400 = 300 ≠ 250 (both violate the first law) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following processes comes closest to being reversible?

options.text_md: A gas expands extremely slowly against a frictionless piston while in contact with a large reservoir at the same temperature
A balloon bursts and its gas rushes out into the air
A block slides across a rough floor and comes to rest
Hot water is poured into cold water in a bucket and stirred

questions.solution_md: A reversible process must be quasi-static and free of friction and of heat flow across a finite temperature difference. Only the slow, frictionless expansion in contact with a reservoir approaches this; the other three involve sudden expansion, friction and finite-temperature mixing — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two refrigerators X and Y each remove 1200 J of heat from their cold spaces in a given time. X needs 300 J of work for this and Y needs 400 J. Which is the better refrigerator, and why?

options.text_md: Y, because it uses more work and so cools more strongly
They are equally good, because each removes 1200 J
X, because its coefficient of performance is 4 against 3 for Y
X, because its coefficient of performance is 3 and Y’s is 4

questions.solution_md: $\text{COP} = Q_2/W$: for X, $1200/300 = 4$; for Y, $1200/400 = 3$. A larger COP means more heat removed per joule of work — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A heat engine that turned all the heat it absorbed from a single reservoir into work in every cycle would break the first law of thermodynamics.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Such an engine would conserve energy (heat in = work out), so the first law is satisfied; it would break the second law (Kelvin–Planck statement).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator can be greater than 1.

**Reason (R):** The work supplied to a refrigerator is always larger than the heat it removes from its cold space.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: COP = Q₂/W is commonly above 2 for a domestic refrigerator. R is false: W is usually much smaller than Q₂, which is why the COP is large — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A refrigerator running in a closed kitchen releases more heat into the room than it removes from its cold compartment.

**Reason (R):** The heat released to the room equals the heat removed from the cold compartment plus the work supplied to the compressor.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Over a cycle ΔU = 0, so Q₁ = Q₂ + W. Because W > 0, Q₁ > Q₂; R states the energy balance and so explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For a refrigerator, the heat removed from the cold space divided by the work supplied is called its coefficient of ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the coefficient of **performance**, COP = Q₂/W.

questions.stem_md: In each cycle a diesel generator set absorbs 750 kJ of heat from burning fuel and rejects 540 kJ to the exhaust and cooling water. Find its efficiency, in per cent.
questions.solution_md: $W = Q_1 - Q_2 = 750 - 540 = 210$ kJ per cycle, so $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_1} \times 100 = \dfrac{210}{750} \times 100 = 28\%$.

questions.stem_md: A heat engine of efficiency 30% delivers 600 J of work in each cycle. Find the heat it rejects to the cold reservoir in each cycle, in J.
In one hour a domestic refrigerator removes 2.7 MJ of heat from its cold space while its compressor supplies 0.60 MJ of work. Find its coefficient of performance.
A window air-conditioner has a coefficient of performance of 3.2 and its compressor takes 1.5 kW of power, all of it used as work. Find the rate at which it releases heat to the outdoors, in kW.
questions.solution_md: Heat removed from the room per second $Q_2 = \text{COP} \times W = 3.2 \times 1.5 = 4.8$ kW. Heat released outdoors $Q_1 = Q_2 + W = 4.8 + 1.5 = 6.3$ kW.

questions.stem_md: A heat engine of efficiency 24% takes in 2500 J of heat from the hot reservoir in each cycle and completes 40 cycles every second. Find the power it delivers, in kW.
questions.solution_md: Work per cycle $W = \eta Q_1 = 0.24 \times 2500 = 600$ J. Power $= 600 \times 40$ J/s $= 24000$ W, so $P = 24$ kW.

questions.stem_md: State the Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics and say what it implies for the efficiency of a heat engine.

answer.model_answer_md: No cyclic device can absorb heat from a **single reservoir** and convert **all** of it into work with no other effect. Hence every heat engine must reject some heat to a colder body, so its efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ is always **less than 1**.

questions.solution_md: Statement; some heat must be rejected, η < 1.

marking_scheme.step: Kelvin–Planck statement: complete conversion of heat from one reservoir into work in a cycle is impossible

questions.stem_md: What is a reversible process? Give one example of a process that is irreversible and state why it is so.

answer.model_answer_md: A **reversible process** can be retraced exactly, so that both the system and its surroundings return to their initial states; it must be quasi-static and free of friction and of heat flow across a finite temperature difference. Example of an irreversible process: a gas rushing into an evacuated chamber, which never collects itself back into one chamber.

questions.solution_md: Definition with conditions; example with reason.

marking_scheme.step: Reversible: retraced exactly, quasi-static, no friction or finite-temperature heat flow
An irreversible example with its reason

questions.stem_md: A hot spoon placed in cold tea cools while the tea warms. Explain why this process is irreversible, how the Clausius statement shows that the spoon cannot spontaneously reheat itself at the tea’s expense, and whether such a reverse process would break the first law.

answer.model_answer_md: Heat flows across a finite temperature difference from the spoon to the tea, and this flow is one-way. The Clausius statement forbids heat from passing from the colder tea to the hotter spoon as the only result. The reverse process would conserve energy, so it would **not** break the first law; it would break the second law.

questions.solution_md: One-way heat flow; Clausius forbids reverse; first law is not violated.

marking_scheme.step: Heat flows across a finite temperature gap; the process is one-way (irreversible)
Clausius: heat cannot pass from cold to hot as the only result
The reverse conserves energy, so it breaks the second law, not the first

questions.stem_md: Describe how a heat engine works, using the heat Q₁ absorbed, the heat Q₂ rejected and the work W done in a cycle. Obtain its efficiency and explain why it cannot be 1.

answer.model_answer_md: The engine absorbs heat $Q_1$ from a hot reservoir, converts part of it into useful work $W$ and rejects the remaining heat $Q_2$ to a cold reservoir. Over a complete cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so $W = Q_1 - Q_2$, and the efficiency is the fraction of the absorbed heat turned into work: $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_1} = 1 - \dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1}$. For $\eta = 1$ we would need $Q_2 = 0$, which the Kelvin–Planck statement forbids.

questions.solution_md: W = Q₁ − Q₂; η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁; η = 1 forbidden.

marking_scheme.step: Q₁ in, W out, Q₂ rejected; W = Q₁ − Q₂ (ΔU = 0)
η = 1 needs Q₂ = 0, which the second law forbids

questions.stem_md: (a) State the first law of thermodynamics and the sign convention you use. (b) A monatomic ideal gas, for which ΔU = (3/2)Δ(PV), is taken from state A (1.0 L, 300 kPa) to state B (4.0 L, 100 kPa) along three paths: path I expands at constant pressure to 4.0 L and then cools at constant volume to 100 kPa; path II cools at constant volume to 100 kPa and then expands at constant pressure to 4.0 L; path III is a straight line from A to B. Find (i) the work done by the gas along each path, (ii) the change in its internal energy, and (iii) the heat absorbed along each path. (c) What do your results show about W, Q and ΔU?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **First law:** $\Delta U = Q - W$, the heat $Q$ supplied to the system minus the work $W$ done by it equals the increase in internal energy; $Q$ is positive into the system and $W$ is positive when the system does work.

(b)(i) Work = area under the path on the P–V diagram (kPa × L = J). Path I: $W = P\,\Delta V = 300 \times 3 = 900$ J. Path II: $W = 100 \times 3 = 300$ J. Path III: trapezoid, $W = \tfrac{1}{2}(300 + 100) \times 3 = 600$ J.

(ii) $\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}(P_BV_B - P_AV_A) = \tfrac{3}{2}(400 - 300) = 150$ J, the same for every path.

(iii) $Q = \Delta U + W$: path I $= 1050$ J, path II $= 450$ J, path III $= 750$ J.

(c) $\Delta U$ depends only on the end states, but $W$ and $Q$ depend on the path.

questions.solution_md: First law; W = 900, 300, 600 J; ΔU = 150 J; Q = 1050, 450, 750 J; only ΔU is path independent.

marking_scheme.step: First law ΔU = Q − W with the sign convention
Work: 900 J, 300 J and 600 J from the areas
Heat: Q = ΔU + W = 1050 J, 450 J, 750 J

questions.stem_md: (a) Using the first law and the ideal gas equation, derive Cp − Cv = R for one mole of an ideal gas. (b) Two moles of a diatomic ideal gas (Cv = 5R/2, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) are heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 360 K. Find (i) the heat absorbed, (ii) the increase in internal energy and (iii) the work done by the gas.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Heat one mole at constant pressure through $\Delta T$. By the first law, $C_p\Delta T = \Delta U + P\Delta V$. For an ideal gas $\Delta U = C_v\Delta T$ for any process. From $PV = RT$ at constant $P$, $P\Delta V = R\Delta T$. So $C_p\Delta T = C_v\Delta T + R\Delta T$, that is $C_p - C_v = R$.

(b) $C_v = \tfrac{5}{2}R = 20.785$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $C_p = C_v + R = 29.099$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $\Delta T = 60$ K.

(i) $Q = nC_p\Delta T = 2 \times 29.099 \times 60 \approx 3492$ J.

(ii) $\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T = 2 \times 20.785 \times 60 \approx 2494$ J.

(iii) $W = nR\Delta T = 2 \times 8.314 \times 60 \approx 997.7$ J. Check: $Q - W \approx 2494$ J $= \Delta U$.

questions.solution_md: Derivation; Cp = 29.10; Q ≈ 3492 J, ΔU ≈ 2494 J, W ≈ 997.7 J.

marking_scheme.step: First law at constant pressure: CpΔT = ΔU + PΔV
ΔU = CvΔT and PΔV = RΔT give Cp − Cv = R

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that the work done by n moles of an ideal gas expanding isothermally at temperature T from V₁ to V₂ is nRT ln(V₂/V₁). (b) Show that in an adiabatic expansion the work done is (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1). (c) One mole of a monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3, Cv = 3R/2, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 300 K doubles its volume, once isothermally and once adiabatically. Find the work done in each case and the final temperature in the adiabatic case.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $P = nRT/V$, so $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2}\dfrac{nRT}{V}\,dV = nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$.

(b) Along an adiabat $PV^{\gamma} = K$, so $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} K V^{-\gamma}\,dV = \dfrac{K}{1-\gamma}\left(V_2^{1-\gamma} - V_1^{1-\gamma}\right) = \dfrac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{1-\gamma} = \dfrac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1}$.

(c) Isothermal: $nRT = 2494.2$ J, so $W = 2494.2 \times \ln 2 \approx 1729$ J.

Adiabatic: $T_2 = T_1\left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma-1} = 300 \times \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2/3} \approx 189.0$ K, and $W = nC_v(T_1 - T_2) = \tfrac{3}{2} \times 8.314 \times (300 - 189.0) \approx 1384$ J.

The isothermal work is larger: the adiabatic gas cools as it expands.

questions.solution_md: Integrals; W_iso ≈ 1729 J; T₂ ≈ 189.0 K; W_adi ≈ 1384 J.

marking_scheme.step: W_adi = nCv(T₁ − T₂) ≈ 1384 J, less than W_iso

questions.stem_md: (a) What is a cyclic process? State the change in internal energy over a cycle and the relation between the net heat and the net work. (b) A monatomic ideal gas (Cv = 3R/2) is taken round the cycle A→B→C→D→A on a P–V diagram: A (1.0 L, 200 kPa), B (1.0 L, 500 kPa), C (3.0 L, 500 kPa), D (3.0 L, 200 kPa), with AB and CD at constant volume and BC and DA at constant pressure. Find (i) the net work done by the gas, (ii) the heat absorbed, (iii) the heat rejected, and (iv) the efficiency of this engine.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **cyclic process** returns the system to its initial state. Then $\Delta U = 0$, so the net heat absorbed equals the net work done, which is the area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram.

(b)(i) $W = (500 - 200) \times (3.0 - 1.0) = 600$ J (the loop is clockwise, so positive).

(ii) AB (constant V): $Q = \tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(PV) = \tfrac{3}{2}(500 - 200) = 450$ J. BC (constant P): $Q = \tfrac{5}{2}P\Delta V = \tfrac{5}{2} \times 500 \times 2 = 2500$ J. Heat absorbed $Q_1 = 450 + 2500 = 2950$ J.

(iii) CD: $Q = -1350$ J; DA: $Q = -1000$ J. Heat rejected $Q_2 = 2350$ J. Check: $Q_1 - Q_2 = 600 = W$.

(iv) $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_1} = \dfrac{600}{2950} \approx 20.3\%$.

questions.solution_md: ΔU = 0 in a cycle; W = 600 J; Q_in = 2950 J; Q_out = 2350 J; η ≈ 20.3%.

marking_scheme.step: Cyclic process: ΔU = 0, so net heat = net work = area of the loop
Heat absorbed on AB and BC: 450 + 2500 = 2950 J
Heat rejected on CD and DA = 2350 J (Q₁ − Q₂ = W)

questions.stem_md: (a) State the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements of the second law of thermodynamics. (b) A refrigerator removes 840 J of heat from its cold chamber in each cycle while 210 J of work is supplied to it. Find its coefficient of performance and the heat it releases to the surroundings per cycle. (c) A heat engine absorbs 1500 J and rejects 1100 J per cycle. Find its efficiency. (d) Explain why the efficiency of an engine is always less than 1 while the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator can exceed 1.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Kelvin–Planck:** no cyclic device can absorb heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work with no other effect. **Clausius:** no cyclic device can have, as its only result, the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter body.

(b) $\text{COP} = \dfrac{Q_2}{W} = \dfrac{840}{210} = 4$. Heat released $Q_1 = Q_2 + W = 840 + 210 = 1050$ J.

(c) $W = Q_1 - Q_2 = 1500 - 1100 = 400$ J, so $\eta = \dfrac{400}{1500} \approx 26.7\%$.

(d) $\eta = 1 - Q_2/Q_1$ reaches 1 only if $Q_2 = 0$, which Kelvin–Planck forbids. COP $= Q_2/W$ compares the heat moved with the work used, and moving heat takes much less work than the heat moved, so it can exceed 1.

questions.solution_md: Statements; COP = 4.0 and Q₁ = 1050 J; η ≈ 26.7%; η < 1 but COP > 1 possible.

marking_scheme.step: η = 1 needs Q₂ = 0 (forbidden); COP = Q₂/W has no such bound

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** 614 K

**(c)** (i) The stroke is adiabatic, with $Q = 0$, so by the first law all the work done on the air goes into its internal energy: the work done on the air equals the rise in its internal energy, $W_\text{on} = nC_v(T_2 - T_1) = 0.02 \times 20.785 \times (614.3 - 300) \approx 131$ J.

answer.model_answer_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) Trial 1 is nearly isothermal and trial 2 is nearly adiabatic

**(b)** 13.8 J

**(c)** (i) In trial 2 no heat escapes, so the work done on the air raises its internal energy and its temperature. Since $PV = nRT$, the final pressure is higher at the same volume. In trial 1 the temperature stays at 300 K, so the pressure is lower.

(ii) Work is the area under the path; paths differ.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) no cyclic engine can convert all the heat it absorbs from a hot source into work (Kelvin–Planck statement)

**(b)** 30 %

**(c)** (i) In a steady cycle the energy balance per second is $W = Q_1 - Q_2$, so the heat that is not delivered as electrical power is carried away by the cooling water, and the rate of heat rejection is $Q_2 = 1500 - 450 = 1050$ MW, that is, 1050 MJ every second.

**OR** (ii) The claim is **wrong**. Friction and heat leaks lower the efficiency of a real plant, but even without them the Kelvin–Planck statement forbids converting all the heat from the hot source into work. Some heat must be rejected to a colder body, so $\eta < 1$ always.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Energy is conserved, so the heat not turned into work must go somewhere. The second law (Kelvin–Planck statement) says some heat must be rejected to a colder body in every cycle — option (b).

**(b)** $\eta = \dfrac{\text{power output}}{\text{heat input rate}} \times 100 = \dfrac{450}{1500} \times 100 = 30\%$.

**(c)** (i) Q₂ = 1500 − 450 = 1050 MW.

(ii) Kelvin–Planck forbids 100%.
